column2: Take the line y equals x, from zero to one. Square every height, and it sags. Higher powers sag further.
Each curve is unbroken, from zero up to one.
Pin one point, x equals nine tenths. Its heights go point nine, point eight one, point seven two nine, down toward zero.
At x equals one, nothing moves. One to any power is one.
So what shape are the curves heading for?
Flat at zero all the way to one, then a single point at height one. Unbroken curves, and a limit that jumps.
A picture of a few curves can't prove that. Arithmetic can. Below one, each new power multiplies the height by the same number less than one.
Now let the point move. On each curve, mark where it crosses half height.
There the curve is at one half and the limit is zero. As the power grows, the crossing creeps toward one, but the gap stays one half.
So it matters who picks the point. Fix it first, and the gap shrinks to zero. Let it move with the curve, and the gap never does.
Shade every x where the curve is still above one half. That's a strip from the crossing up to one, and x equals one belongs to it.
But at one, the curve and the limit are both at height one. The gap there is zero.
So the gap is at least one half only on a strip that starts at the crossing and stops just short of one.
As the power grows, that strip gets narrower.
Once it's thinner than a pixel, is the trouble gone?
No. Stretch the end of the interval sideways, ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times. The strip is still there.
Reset the window to x to the tenth. Raise the power tenfold and stretch tenfold, then again. It looks almost the same. Its width shrinks like point six nine over n, and the strip is never empty.
And the moving point is always inside it, with its gap of one half.
A picture shows a few powers, at finite resolution. What we need is a guarantee for every point at once, and an order for who chooses what.
The guarantee has to answer an old objection. In seventeen thirty four, George Berkeley questioned a step in an argument for how fast a power changes.
Here is that kind of argument for a square, in modern notation. Move x from one half by h, not zero. The height changes by h plus h squared. Divide by h, and the slope is one plus h.
Then the argument lets h vanish, so one plus h becomes one. Berkeley objected that h was something for the division and nothing afterward, yet the result was kept.
So what slope does h equal to zero give?
None. Both points are then the same point, and the change is zero over zero.
One is still the right answer, reached without h ever being zero. Shrink h from both sides, and the slopes close in on one.
For every h within one tenth of zero, other than zero, the slope is within one tenth of one. Any tolerance works the same way, so the limit is one.
This never needs the step Berkeley questioned. Who picks the tolerance, and when, comes next. Whether a limit exists at all is a separate question, for the end.
Make it a game with strict turns. The challenger names a tolerance, epsilon. The defender answers with a window, delta. Then the challenger picks any h in it but zero.
Against one tenth, the defender answers one tenth. Every h the challenger can pick lands in the band, since each slope is as far from one as h is from zero.
Catching some h is not enough. Answer one fifth instead, and point one five lands outside.
A limit leaves zero out. Continuity puts zero in and aims at the value there. Fill the hole with one, and it is continuous. Fill it with one and a half, and no window works.
But if the defender could see h first, could this broken graph still win?
Yes, always, with a window too narrow to hold it. So the window may depend on the tolerance, the point and the curve, never on the later h.

Continuity at x equals one, where the square's domain ends. With tolerance one half, exclude the half height crossing, where the gap is exactly one half. Every x beyond it, up to and including one, passes.
A winning answer covers every input in its window. Finding them is a search that written proofs hide.
A finished proof opens with a choice like delta equals two thirds of epsilon, and never says where it came from. Here is the search.
Start from what the challenger demands. x squared must be within epsilon of a quarter, for every x near one half.
That gap is the distance from one half, times x plus one half.
On the domain, zero to one, x plus one half is never more than three halves. That is the deliberate, generous step.
So a distance below two thirds of epsilon is enough. That is where delta came from.
Against one tenth, about how large could delta be, and still work?
About point zero nine two, where the curve leaves the band. One fifteenth is smaller, and still enough. A window only has to work for every input, not be the widest.

Now read the proof forward, as it is written. Given epsilon, take delta as two thirds of epsilon. For every x in the domain and in the window, the gap is below three halves of delta, which is epsilon.
The search ran backward from the goal. The proof runs forward, and hides it. Next, ways to make that search systematic.
Leave the interval. Take x squared on all real numbers, at two, where it is four.
Let h be x minus two. x squared minus four is h squared plus four h.
On either side, its size is at most h squared plus four times the size of h.
Near two the curve is nearly straight, slope four. Try delta as epsilon over four, one fortieth against one tenth. Does every h in that window pass?
No, but almost. h equal to point zero two four nine moves x squared by point one zero zero two two.
Budget both terms. Adding four completes a square, the size of h plus two, squared, below four plus epsilon.
So delta is the square root of four plus epsilon, minus two, positive for every epsilon. Every h within delta of zero, on either side, keeps the gap below epsilon.
Against one tenth, about point zero two four eight. The usual way first keeps h within one, so x plus two stays below five. Delta is the smaller of one and epsilon over five, point zero two.
Both work. Sprague's note solves the budget instead of capping it. Next, a bound for any polynomial.
Take x cubed plus five x squared near one, where it is six. Put h equal to x minus one.
The change is h cubed plus eight h squared plus thirteen h. Bound its size by adding the three sizes.
Keep the size of h below one. Each higher power is then at most the size of h.
What single multiple of the size of h covers all three terms?
Twenty two. One, eight and thirteen add to twenty two. So choose delta as the smaller of one and epsilon over twenty two.
Every h inside delta, on either side, keeps the change below epsilon.
For any polynomial, expand around the point. Add the sizes of its nonconstant coefficients, and call that C.
If C is positive, use the smaller of one and epsilon over C. If zero, the polynomial is constant. Any positive delta works.
Davis's note supplies a reusable bound, without derivatives. Now return to the curves whose limit jumps.
Return to x to the n, on zero to one. Each fixed point approaches the broken limit.
Fix x, then choose a tolerance. Beyond some stage, every later curve meets it there. The stage may depend on x.
For one half, nine tenths needs stage seven. Point nine nine needs sixty nine. Near the endpoint, the wait grows.
Uniform convergence asks for a stage that works at every point, for every later curve. Choose it before the point.
Keep the tolerance at one half. Can any stage, however late, meet that stronger promise?
No. At any proposed stage, choose its half height crossing. Below one the limit is zero, so the gap is exactly one half, which is not below one half.
The point moves with the stage. This defeats uniform convergence, while each fixed point still converges.
Pointwise allows a separate wait for each point. Uniform requires a shared wait for the whole domain.
Next, that shared wait carries continuity through the limit.
Suppose continuous functions approach a limit uniformly. Fix a point a and a tolerance.
Compare the limit at x and a by taking a detour through a single approximating curve. There are three gaps.
Choose a stage whose curve is within a third of the tolerance everywhere. This controls both outer gaps.
Freeze that curve. Its continuity supplies a window keeping the middle gap below a third, for every x in that window.
Each gap has its budget. Can the total error still reach the full tolerance?
No. The triangle inequality adds the gaps, each strictly below a third. Their sum is below the full tolerance.
The limit is continuous at a. Since a was arbitrary, it is continuous throughout the domain.
Uniform convergence chose the curve before x, then continuity chose the window.
Uniform convergence is sufficient, not necessary for every continuous limit. Next, test continuity by approaching along sequences.
Continuity at a sends every sequence approaching a to outputs approaching f of a.
For our broken limit, choose one minus one over n. These inputs approach one from below.
Every output is zero, but the endpoint value is one. This sequence exposes the discontinuity.
Can checking several good sequences establish continuity?
No. Every sequence must work. If continuity fails, some tolerance defeats every window.
Use windows of radius one over n. Choose a failing input in each. Inputs approach a, and output errors stay at least that tolerance.
A caution about windows. The square root is continuous at zero, yet its widest window is epsilon squared.
Halve the tolerance, and that window shrinks to a quarter, so no fixed fraction of epsilon works for every tolerance.
Now take a whole set of outputs. Its preimage collects every input landing in it. No inverse function is needed.
Take x squared on the real line. Select outputs strictly between one and nine.
Must those inputs form a single piece?
No. Two open intervals, one negative and one positive. Their ends square to exactly one or nine, so they are left out.

Open means every point has a little interval around it inside the set. For continuity, every open output set has an open preimage. Around each output, fit a band inside the set. Continuity supplies a window around its input, inside the preimage.
Conversely, take the band within epsilon of f of a. Its open preimage contains a whole window around a. That window gives delta.
A jump fails. The preimage starts at zero, but every interval around zero holds negative inputs, which land outside. So it is not open.
The domain matters. For square root on nonnegative inputs, this preimage is open within its domain, though not in the real line.
Open sets express the same continuity promise. Finally, what does that promise leave unanswered?
Continuity cannot promise that every value you want exists. Take q squared minus two, on the rational numbers from one to two, ends included.
The endpoint values have opposite signs, minus one and two.
This function is continuous. The output difference is at most four times the input difference, so epsilon over four works as delta.
Must a zero exist in this rational domain?
No. Its positive zero would be the square root of two, which is irrational. A fraction in lowest terms would force both its numerator and denominator to be even.
Bisection keeps rational endpoints on opposite sides and halves their distance. They approach the same real number, but that number is missing from our domain.
On a closed real interval, completeness supplies the missing point. Continuity then makes its function value zero.
Definitions specify the challenge. Estimates build a response. Existence needs its own hypotheses.
Ask who chooses what, and when. Getting closer is useful. Knowing exactly what it promises is stronger.
